excerpt: Growing up in the Philippines, the word "ketong" meant shame and total isolation. Decades later, discovering the story of WWII resistance hero Joey Guerrero revealed how the very mark of social exile became a secret weapon that saved thousands of lives.
author: Lexi Zotomayor
bodyText:
In the Philippines, *ketong* was never just a disease; it was a sentence. Long before anyone knew the medical terms for skin lesions, the word was used to carve people out of society. Bullying on the playground was built around it. Severe eczema, scabies, or contact dermatitis were all tagged with the same fearful label. We grew up under a canopy of old wives’ tales—warned that taking a shower right after pressing clothes would somehow bring the affliction upon you. Fear was passed down like a family heirloom.

That was the only lens I had for the word until I stumbled across Ben Montgomery’s *The Leper Spy*.

That was how I learned about Josephina “Joey” Guerrero. And it left me asking an uncomfortable question: *How did I grow up in the Philippines without ever hearing her name?*

![](/assets/uploads/cms/jguerrero1.jpg)

Joey contracted leprosy as a young woman. The diagnosis destroyed her life in an instant. Her husband left, taking their young daughter, and she was cast out to the fringes of society. When World War II broke out and the Japanese military occupied the islands, her exile took an unexpected turn.

The occupying forces harbored a deep, almost hysterical terror of leprosy. Sentries would not go near her. The very mark that had stripped Joey of her place in the world became her shield. She could walk through military checkpoints untouched, unseen, and unsearched.

She joined the underground resistance. Her most critical mission involved carrying a hidden map detailing the minefields guarding the approach to Manila. Hidden on her person, the map moved as she walked for miles through heavily guarded enemy lines. Every footstep carried the risk of discovery, but she kept moving until she reached the American lines.

The map saved thousands of soldiers and civilian captives from planned summary executions.

When the war ended, there were no speeches or parades for Joey. She eventually sought treatment at the Carville leprosarium in the United States and chose to live out her remaining years in quiet obscurity under the name Joey Leaumax.

Her story completely upended how I think about history and who we choose to remember. Joey took the very rejection meant to erase her and wore it as a cloak—turning a cruel exile into a shield that saved a nation.

![Joey receives treatment at the leprosarium in Carville, Louisiana.](/assets/uploads/cms/joeyguerrerogettingtreatment.jpg "Joey receives treatment at the leprosarium in Carville, Louisiana.")
title: The Cloak
